summary: Likely synthetic: the face looks machine-made, and the AI-image detector found generator fingerprints.

tests.name: AI-Generated Image Detector
tests.finding: Generator fingerprints detected; 4 of 9 patches look synthetic.
tests.explain: A vision transformer trained on millions of real photos and images from thousands of generators (GANs, diffusion models, commercial apps) has learnt the tiny statistical fingerprints generators leave in texture and colour. It outputs a probability; we also scan 9 overlapping patches to see where it reacts.

tests.name: AI Face Analysis
tests.finding: The face shows synthetic skin and detail patterns.
tests.explain: A small neural network (YuNet) finds each face; the same AI-image detector is then zoomed onto a crop of that face. It reliably catches faces that were generated whole (GANs, diffusion), but it was not trained on face-swaps or lip-sync, so a well-blended swap of a real face can pass as real.

tests.name: Error Level Analysis
tests.finding: Error levels look even across the image; no area stands out.
tests.explain: ELA re-saves the picture as a JPEG at a fixed quality and measures how much each pixel changes. Brighter areas changed more: fine detail and edges always glow, but a region with a different compression history can glow too. It is a map for human eyes; on its own it rarely proves an edit.

tests.name: Noise Residual Consistency
tests.finding: Camera-like sensor grain, consistent across the whole image.
tests.explain: A real camera sensor leaves a fine, even grain over the whole picture. Subtracting a denoised copy isolates that grain; we measure its strength block by block. Generated images often have too little grain - but so do phone photos after noise reduction, webcams and video stills, so that is weak evidence.

tests.name: Frequency Spectrum (FFT)
tests.finding: Natural spectrum with camera-like fine detail; no grid artefacts.
tests.explain: The Fourier transform splits an image into waves of different spatial frequency. Camera photos keep fine detail and sensor grain right up to the highest frequencies, while generators tend to be too smooth there; their up-sampling layers can also leave periodic grid peaks in the spectrum.

tests.name: JPEG Quantisation Tables
tests.finding: Quality 95 with standard software tables; re-saved by an app or editor.
tests.explain: JPEG compression rounds each 8x8 block's frequency components by amounts listed in quantisation tables. Phone cameras use their own tables, whereas editors, apps and AI tools re-save with standard tables; re-saving an already-compressed JPEG also leaves periodic gaps in the DCT histogram.

tests.name: Metadata & Provenance
tests.finding: No metadata at all; stripped by an app, or never a camera photo.
tests.explain: Digital files carry hidden labels: cameras record make, model, lens and capture time in EXIF, while many AI tools embed their prompt, software name or a C2PA 'content credential'. Metadata is easy to strip or fake, so it is supporting evidence rather than proof.

_showcase.note: Unedited engine report for this exhibit; PNG charts stored as lossless WebP.
